newsitem.title: FRANCE: New front opens in French monetary policy fight.
newsitem.headline: New front opens in French monetary policy fight.

text.p: A new front in France's running battle over the "franc fort" (strong franc) policy has opened with the impending replacement of two members of the Bank of France's powerful policy-setting council.

France's European Union partners and financial markets are watching the fight closely because because of fears President Jacques Chirac may try to tilt the balance of power on the nine-member council toward a softer monetary policy.

The council sets official interest rates, the main tool in France's defence of the franc fort policy, which successive governments have tenaciously defended as key to their ambitions to join a single European Union currency when it is launched on January 1, 1999.
Supporters of the policy are believed to hold a six-to-three majority on the council.
Both members whose mandates are expiring are in the majority and their replacements could have a decisive effect in tilting the balance towards a softer monetary policy.
The mandates of ex-journalist Jean Boissonnat and banker Bruno de Maulde expire on January 6.
Their replacements will be chosen from a list of six names submitted to the government by the heads of the upper and lower houses of parliament and the Economic and Social Council (CES).
The newspaper Le Monde said on Wednesday Chirac had intervened personally to get Pierre Guillen, described by newspapers as against the franc fort, on the list of candidates.
Guillen is one of two candidates proposed by CES head Jean Matteoli for the council.
The other is Jean-Rene Bernard, formerly head of regional bank CIC and deputy governor of property bank Credit Foncier. He is also reported to be close to Chirac.
Guillen denied on Wednesday he was against a single currency but said he would have liked to see interest rates fall faster.
"I am neither anti-Maastricht nor against a single currency," Guillen told Reuters in an interview. "I voted for the Maastricht treaty, you can check."
He added: "Like many industrialists, I wanted interest rates to come down a little bit faster, but that's an opinion that is an opinion of a representative of industry and that's it."
Senate head Rene Monory said earlier on Wednesday that he wanted to reappoint Boissonnat along with Pierre Achard, economic counsellor at the French embassy in Bonn.

Sources familiar with the nominating process said National Assembly head Philippe Seguin had put forward Robert Pelletier, formerly managing director of the Association of Credit Establishments (Afec) and Alain Prate, former vice-president of the European Investment Bank (EIB).

But he was not expecting his candidates to be chosen since, under the conventions governing the Bank of France nomination procedures, it was up to Matteoli and Monory to submit nominations this time round.

The franc fort has been the source of fierce debate over the last decade, a debate which erupted again last month when former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing called for a weaker franc to boost economic growth and cut record unemployment.
His call revived criticism of the franc fort, drawing public support from inside the government's ruling centre-right coalition and even from members of the Bank's council itself.

Under the terms of the law making the Bank of France independent in 1994, Bank council members must be named by the French cabinet on the basis of a list submitted by the presidents of the Senate, National Assembly and CES.
The list is submitted for comment to the Bank of France council. The law requires replacements to be named at least eight days before the expiry of their mandate.
